title: Turnus ad arma. Camilla
titleEn: Turnus to Arms; Camilla's Offer — Aeneid XI.445–531
about: While Latinus's council is still quarrelling, a messenger bursts in: Aeneas has broken camp, and the Trojans and their Etruscan allies are marching down from the Tiber across the plain. The city is thrown into uproar, the young men shouting for arms, the elders weeping and wavering, a din Virgil compares to birds settling in a grove or swans crying on the marshes of the Po. Turnus seizes his moment with a sneer (let them sit and praise peace while the enemy overruns the kingdom) and hurries out, giving orders as he goes to Volusus, Messapus and Coras. Latinus abandons his plan and blames himself for not having taken Aeneas as son-in-law; the Latins man the walls, dig trenches and haul up stones, and matrons and boys stand along the ramparts. The queen goes up with the matrons and Lavinia to the temple of Pallas and they pray, as the Trojan women once prayed to Athena in the Iliad, for the Phrygian robber to fall before their gates. Turnus arms and runs down from the citadel in his gold and bronze, like a stallion breaking loose for the pastures and the river. At the gates Camilla, queen of the Volscians, leaps from her horse and offers to meet the Trojan and Etruscan cavalry alone. Turnus gives her command of the horse, with Messapus, and tells her his own plan: Aeneas is crossing the hills by a mountain track, and Turnus will ambush him in a wooded defile. Virgil describes the valley and the hidden plateau above it, and Turnus goes and takes up his position there.

sentences.t:
Illi haec inter se dubiis de rebus agebant
certantes; castra Aeneas aciemque movebat:
sentences.l:
They were these things among themselves on doubtful matters debating,
contending; his camp Aeneas and his battle-line was moving:
sentences.i: So they argued among themselves, contending over a question that hung in the balance; and all the while Aeneas was moving his camp and his line of battle:
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Illi', Latinus and his council, still at the quarrel of the last part. 'haec… agebant', 'were debating these things'; 'dubiis de rebus', 'in a doubtful state of affairs', a crisis whose outcome is unclear. The two clauses stand side by side with no connective (asyndeton): the effect is 'while they talked, Aeneas marched'. 'castra movere', the regular Roman phrase for breaking camp to march. The imperfects set the scene for the sudden present of 448. Elisions 'Ill(i) haec', 'castr(a) Aeneas'.

sentences.t:
nuntius ingenti per regia tecta tumultu
ecce ruit magnisque urbem terroribus implet,
instructos acie Tiberino a flumine Teucros
Tyrrhenamque manum totis descendere campis.
sentences.l:
a messenger, amid huge uproar, through the royal halls,
look, rushes, and with great terrors fills the city:
the Teucrians, drawn up in battle-line, from the Tiber river,
and the Tyrrhenian band over all the plains are coming down.
sentences.i: and look, a messenger comes running through the palace amid a great uproar and fills the city with alarm: the Trojans, he reports, are coming down from the Tiber in battle order, and the Etruscan force with them, across the whole breadth of the plain.
sentences.n: 'ecce', 'look!', and the vivid presents 'ruit… implet' break into the imperfects. 'ingenti… tumultu', framing the line, ablative of attendant circumstance. The accusative and infinitive 'Teucros… descendere' depends on the idea of reporting contained in 'nuntius'; no verb of saying is expressed. 'Tiberino a flumine', from the Trojan camp near the Tiber's mouth. 'Tyrrhenam manum', the Etruscan allies who joined Aeneas under Tarchon in Book X. 'totis… campis', 'over all the plains', local ablative. Elisions 'magnisqu(e) urbem', 'Tiberin(o) a'.

sentences.t:
Extemplo turbati animi concussaque vulgi
pectora et adrectae stimulis haud mollibus irae.
sentences.l:
At once disturbed were their minds, and shaken the common people's
hearts, and roused by goads not gentle their angers.
sentences.i: At once their spirits were thrown into confusion, the hearts of the common people were shaken, and their anger was roused by goads that were anything but gentle.
sentences.n: No verb: 'sunt' is understood with all three participles, an ellipsis natural in quick narrative. 'vulgi', the common people, as opposed to the council. 'adrectae', Greenough's spelling with the prefix left unassimilated (the familiar form is 'arrectae'), from 'arrigo', 'raise up', of anger 'pricked up' like a beast's ears. You will meet these 'ad-' spellings all through this part: 'adrepto', 'adceperit', 'adsciverit', 'adcinxerat', 'adcommoda'. 'stimulis haud mollibus', 'by goads not soft', litotes for sharp ones. Elisions 'turbat(i) animi', 'pector(a) et'.

sentences.t:
Arma manu trepidi poscunt, fremit arma iuventus,
flent maesti mussantque patres.
sentences.l:
For arms with the hand, alarmed, they call; roars 'arms!' the youth;
weep, sorrowing, and mutter the fathers.
sentences.i: In their alarm they reach out and clamour for weapons, the young men roar for war, while the elders weep in sorrow and mutter their doubts.
sentences.n: 'Arma… arma', anaphora, the word repeated at each half of the line. 'manu poscunt', 'demand with the hand', with gestures as well as voices. 'trepidi', 'in a flurry, alarmed'. 'fremit arma', 'roars arms', an internal accusative: the shout is the word itself (Turnus himself 'arma amens fremit' at VII.460). 'patres', the elders and councillors, who 'mussant', 'mutter', unable to decide: young against old. The three clauses run without connectives, quickening the pace. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Hic undique clamor
dissensu vario magnus se tollit in auras
haud secus atque alto in luco cum forte catervae
consedere avium piscosove amne Padusae
dant sonitum rauci per stagna loquacia cycni.
sentences.l:
Here on every side a clamour,
with varied discord, great, raises itself into the airs,
not otherwise than when in a deep grove by chance the flocks
of birds have settled, or on the fish-filled river Padusa
give out sound the hoarse swans through the talkative pools.
sentences.i: Then on every side a great clamour of discordant voices rises into the air, just as when flocks of birds happen to settle in a deep grove, or hoarse swans send their cries over the chattering pools of the Padusa, rich in fish.
sentences.n: 'Hic', 'at this point'. 'dissensu vario', 'with varied disagreement', ablative of manner. The simile is introduced by 'haud secus atque… cum', 'not otherwise than when'. 'consedere' = 'consederunt', the perfect in '-ere' (you will see this constantly). 'piscosove amne Padusae', '-ve', 'or'; the Padusa was a channel of the Po delta near Ravenna, famous for swans. 'stagna loquacia', 'chattering pools', the birds' noise given to the water. Homeric model: the Greek host pouring onto the plain like geese, cranes and long-necked swans by the Cayster (Iliad II.459–466, from memory). Elisions 'atqu(e) alto', 'alt(o) in', 'conseder(e) avium', 'piscosov(e) amne'.

sentences.t:
“Immo, ait, O cives adrepto tempore, Turnus,”
“cogite concilium et pacem laudate sedentes:
illi armis in regna ruunt. ”Nec plura locutus
corripuit sese et tectis citus extulit altis.
sentences.l:
“Oh yes,” says Turnus, seizing the moment, “citizens,
call a council and, sitting there, praise peace:
they with arms on the kingdom are rushing.” No more having spoken
he snatched himself up and swiftly carried himself out of the high halls.
sentences.i: “Oh yes, citizens,” said Turnus, seizing his moment, “call your council and sit there praising peace: they are rushing on the kingdom in arms.” Without another word he sprang up and hurried out of the lofty palace.
sentences.n: The print has '“Immo, ait, O cives adrepto tempore, Turnus,”', with 'ait' and 'Turnus' inside the marks, a second opening mark before 'cogite', and 'ruunt. ”Nec' at 461 (as 'vale. ”Nec', 11.98): misprints for a speech 'Immo… O cives… ruunt.' with 'ait… adrepto tempore, Turnus' outside it, corrected here. 'Immo', 'nay rather', bitterly ironic: by all means keep talking. 'adrepto tempore', ablative absolute, 'the moment seized'. 'cogite… laudate', mocking imperatives, 'cogite concilium' throwing back Latinus's own 'cogere concilium' (304); 'sedentes', 'sitting', the posture of a council that talks while others act. 'illi', the enemy; 'in regna', poetic plural. 'corripuit sese', 'snatched himself up'. Elisions 'Imm(o) ait', 'concili(um) et', 'ill(i) armis', 'ses(e) et'.

sentences.t:
“Tu, Voluse, armari Volscorum edice maniplos,
“duc, ait, et Rutulos.
sentences.l:
“You, Volusus, the Volscians' companies to arm give order,
and lead out,” he says, “the Rutulians too.
sentences.i: “Volusus,” he said, “give orders for the Volscian companies to arm, and lead out the Rutulians as well.
sentences.n: The print has '“duc, ait, et Rutulos' at the start of 464, a misprint (as '“Ite, ait,' at 11.24) for 'duc,” ait, “et Rutulos', corrected here: Turnus's speech is already running from 463 and only breaks off for 'ait'. 'Voluse', vocative of Volusus, a Volscian captain. 'armari… edice maniplos', 'proclaim that the companies be armed', accusative and passive infinitive. The Latin Library's 'maniplis' (dative, 'give the companies orders to arm') changes the construction, hardly the sense. 'maniplos', syncopated 'manipulos', the only form that fits the verse. 'et Rutulos', 'the Rutulians too', 'et' meaning 'also'. Elisions 'Volus(e) armari', 'Volscor(um) edice'.

sentences.t:
Equitem Messapus in armis
et cum fratre Coras latis diffundite campis.
Pars aditus urbis firmet turrisque capessat,
cetera, qua iusso, mecum manus inferat arma.”
sentences.l:
The cavalry, Messapus, in arms,
and with your brother, Coras, over the broad plains spread out.
Part, the approaches of the city let it secure and the towers occupy;
the rest, where I shall have ordered, with me let the band carry arms.”
sentences.i: Messapus, and you, Coras, with your brother, deploy the cavalry in arms across the broad plains. Let one part hold the approaches to the city and man the towers; let the rest of the force carry the attack with me wherever I give the word.”
sentences.n: 'Messapus… Coras… diffundite', nominatives with a plural imperative, the nominative doing duty for the vocative, common in verse. 'Equitem', collective singular, 'the cavalry'. Coras and his twin Catillus, Argive warriors from Tibur, the town named after their brother Tiburtus, appeared in the catalogue of Book VII (670–677). 'firmet… capessat', jussive subjunctives agreeing with 'Pars'; the Latin Library's plural 'firment… capessant' (agreement by sense) changes nothing in meaning. 'turris', '-is' accusative plural. 'qua iusso' = 'qua iussero', 'where I shall have ordered', an old future perfect in '-so', surviving in Virgil's day in archaic and legal language (compare 'faxo'). 'inferat arma', 'carry the attack'. No elisions.

sentences.t: Ilicet in muros tota discurritur urbe.
sentences.l: At once onto the walls through the whole city there is running everywhere.
sentences.i: At once there is a rush to the walls from every quarter of the city.
sentences.n: 'Ilicet', 'at once'; it was originally 'ire licet', 'you may go', the formula that dismissed a Roman court or assembly, and that origin suits the moment, since the council is breaking up. 'discurritur', impersonal passive, 'there is running in all directions': the action without the actors, a favourite device for crowds. 'tota… urbe', local ablative without 'in'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Consilium ipse pater et magna incepta Latinus
deserit ac tristi turbatus tempore differt
multaque se incusat, qui non adceperit ultro
Dardanium Aenean generumque adsciverit urbi.
sentences.l:
His plan, himself, the father, and his great undertakings Latinus
abandons, and, by the gloomy time troubled, puts them off,
and much he accuses himself, who did not receive of his own accord
Dardanian Aeneas and adopt him as son-in-law for the city.
sentences.i: Father Latinus himself abandons his plan and his great design and, shaken by this grim hour, puts it off, and he blames himself again and again for not having welcomed Dardanian Aeneas of his own free will and taken him into the city as his son-in-law.
sentences.n: 'Consilium… et magna incepta', his peace proposal and the embassy with gifts (302–335). The Latin Library has 'concilium', 'he leaves the council', which changes the sense: there the meeting breaks up; here the plan is given up, and 'differt', 'puts off', suits a plan. 'pater', a title of respect for the king; its last syllable is lengthened at the pause in the third foot, a licence Virgil allows at the caesura. 'multa se incusat', 'accuses himself much', 'multa' an internal accusative. 'qui non adceperit', causal relative with the subjunctive, 'since he had not received'; 'adceperit… adsciverit' are Greenough's spellings of 'acceperit… asciverit'. 'ultro', 'unasked'. 'Aenean', Greek accusative. 'urbi', 'for the city'. Elisions 'Consili(um) ipse', 'magn(a) incepta', 's(e) incusat', 'Dardani(um) Aenean', 'generumqu(e) adsciverit'.

sentences.t:
Praefodiunt alii portas aut saxa sudesque
subvectant.
sentences.l:
Dig before the gates some, or rocks and stakes
carry up.
sentences.i: Some dig trenches before the gates, others bring up stones and stakes.
sentences.n: 'Praefodiunt… portas', 'dig in front of the gates', a rare compound taking the accusative of the thing dug before. 'alii… aut', 'some… or (others)': 'aut' stands where we expect a second 'alii'. 'sudes', sharpened stakes for the defence. 'subvectant', frequentative of 'subveho', 'keep carrying up', the repeated loads. The narrative runs on in vivid presents. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Bello dat signum rauca cruentum
bucina.
sentences.l:
For war gives the signal, hoarse, the bloody one,
the horn.
sentences.i: The hoarse horn sounds the bloody signal for battle.
sentences.n: 'Bello', dative, 'for war'. 'cruentum' agrees with 'signum': the signal is 'bloody' because it begins the bloodshed, a transferred epithet. 'rauca… bucina', the adjective in mid-line and the noun held over to the first word of the next: you wait to hear what instrument it is. The 'bucina' was the curved horn of the Roman camp that sounded the watches; Virgil gives the Latins Roman equipment. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Tum muros varia cinxere corona
matronae puerique: vocat labor ultimus omnis.
sentences.l:
Then the walls, with a varied garland, ringed
the matrons and boys: calls the final toil all.
sentences.i: Then matrons and boys ringed the walls in a motley circle: this last, desperate labour calls on everyone.
sentences.n: 'cinxere' = 'cinxerunt'. 'varia… corona', 'with a varied ring', 'corona' the regular military word for a ring of men round a wall, here a mixed one. 'matronae puerique', the subject held back to the next line. 'labor ultimus', 'the final toil', the crisis that leaves no one out. 'omnis', '-is' accusative plural, 'all'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Nec non ad templum summasque ad Palladis arces
subvehitur magna matrum regina caterva
dona ferens, iuxtaque comes Lavinia virgo,
causa mali tanti, oculos deiecta decoros.
sentences.l:
And also to the temple and to the highest citadel of Pallas
is carried up, with a great throng of matrons, the queen,
gifts bearing, and beside her as companion Lavinia the maiden,
the cause of so great an evil, her eyes cast down, her lovely ones.
sentences.i: The queen too, attended by a great throng of matrons, rides up to the temple of Pallas on the summit of the citadel, bearing gifts, and beside her goes the maiden Lavinia, the cause of all this disaster, her lovely eyes lowered.
sentences.n: 'Nec non', 'and also', two negatives making a strong positive. 'subvehitur', 'is carried up', in a carriage, as Roman matrons rode to festivals. 'regina', Amata, Latinus's queen. 'magna matrum… caterva', ablative of attendant circumstance. Homeric model: Hecuba and the Trojan women carry a robe up to Athena's temple on the citadel and pray to her (Iliad VI.286–311, from memory). 'causa mali tanti', the same words the Sibyl used of a foreign bride (VI.93). 'oculos deiecta decoros', 'cast down as to her lovely eyes', a participle in middle sense with an accusative, on the Greek model. Elision 'summasqu(e) ad'. 'tanti, oculos' is not elided: 'tanti' keeps its long -i in hiatus at the pause and the main caesura (as 'Samo hic', I.16).

sentences.t:
Succedunt matres et templum ture vaporant
et maestas alto fundunt de limine voces:
sentences.l:
Go up the matrons and the temple with incense fill with smoke,
and mournful from the high threshold pour out voices:
sentences.i: The matrons enter, fill the temple with the smoke of incense, and from the lofty threshold pour out their mournful prayers:
sentences.n: 'Succedunt', 'go up to, enter'. 'ture vaporant', 'fill with incense-smoke', 'tus, turis', frankincense. 'alto… de limine', 'from the high threshold': the temple stands at the top of the citadel, and prayers were often spoken at the door before the image. 'maestas… voces', the adjective and noun framing the line. The vivid presents continue. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Armipotens, praeses belli, Tritonia virgo,
frange manu telum Phrygii praedonis et ipsum
pronum sterne solo portisque effunde sub altis.”
sentences.l:
“Mighty in arms, guardian of war, Tritonian maiden,
break with your hand the spear of the Phrygian robber, and himself
headlong lay low on the ground and stretch him out beneath the high gates.”
sentences.i: “Mighty in arms, mistress of war, Tritonian maiden, break with your own hand the spear of the Phrygian robber, throw him headlong to the earth and lay him out dead beneath our lofty gates.”
sentences.n: A prayer in hymn style: titles first ('Armipotens', 'praeses belli', 'Tritonia virgo'), then the requests. 'Tritonia', Minerva (Athena), named from Lake Triton in Libya, her birthplace in one story. 'Phrygii praedonis', 'the Phrygian bandit': Aeneas cast as a second Paris, come to carry off a bride. 'effunde', 'pour out', of a body sprawled in death. The model is Theano's prayer in Iliad VI.305–310 (from memory): break the spear of Diomedes and let him fall before the Scaean gates; Athena refused, and the reader suspects Minerva will too. Elision 'portisqu(e) effunde'.

sentences.t: Cingitur ipse furens certatim in proelia Turnus.
sentences.l: Girds himself, raging, eagerly for battles, Turnus.
sentences.i: Turnus himself, in a fury, arms for battle in eager haste.
sentences.n: Narrative resumes after the matrons' prayer. 'Cingitur', passive in middle sense, 'girds himself', 'arms'. 'ipse', in contrast with the women at their prayers. 'furens', the word that follows Turnus through these books. 'certatim', usually 'in rivalry', of several people vying; of one man it means 'with all eagerness', as if racing the rest. 'in proelia', poetic plural. The subject is held to the last word of the line. Elision 'certati(m) in'.

sentences.t:
Iamque adeo rutilum thoraca indutus aenis
horrebat squamis surasque incluserat auro,
tempora nudus adhuc, laterique adcinxerat ensem
fulgebatque alta decurrens aureus arce,
exsultatque animis et spe iam praecipit hostem:
sentences.l:
And now indeed, the ruddy breastplate having put on, with bronze
he bristled, scales, and his calves he had enclosed in gold,
his temples bare as yet, and to his side he had girded his sword,
and he gleamed, from the high running down, golden, citadel,
and exults in spirit, and in hope already seizes in advance the enemy:
sentences.i: And now he had put on his ruddy breastplate and bristled with scales of bronze, he had sheathed his legs in gold, his head still bare, and had belted his sword to his side, and he flashed all golden as he ran down from the high citadel, exulting in his heart and in his hopes already closing with the enemy:
sentences.n: 'Iamque adeo', 'and now indeed'. 'thoraca', Greek accusative of 'thorax', object of 'indutus', 'having put on', a passive participle in middle sense. 'aenis… squamis', 'with bronze scales', scale-armour, 'aenis' three syllables, a-e-nis; 'horrebat', 'bristled'. 'suras… auro', golden greaves. 'tempora nudus', 'bare as to the temples', Greek accusative of respect: no helmet yet. 'adcinxerat', Greenough's 'accinxerat'. 'aureus', 'golden', said of the man himself. Imperfects ('horrebat', 'fulgebat') and pluperfects ('incluserat', 'adcinxerat') give way to the vivid present 'exsultat… praecipit'; 'praecipit hostem', 'grasps the enemy in advance', in imagination. Elisions 'Iamqu(e) adeo', 'thorac(a) indutus', 'surasqu(e) incluserat', 'lateriqu(e) adcinxerat', 'fulgebatqu(e) alta', 'exsultatqu(e) animis'.

sentences.t:
qualis ubi abruptis fugit praesaepia vinclis
tandem liber equus campoque potitus aperto
sentences.l:
just as when, his tethers broken, has fled the stalls
at last free a horse, and of the plain having gained possession, the open one,
sentences.i: just as a horse, when he has snapped his halter and bolted from the stable, free at last and master of the open plain,
sentences.n: Greenough prints the simile as one six-line period with no stop inside it, so it is divided here, without a mark, where the horse reaches the plain and the two alternatives ('aut… aut') begin. 'qualis', 'such as', answering Turnus. 'fugit' is perfect, 'fūgit' (the metre needs the long u), the instant of breaking loose; the presents 'tendit… emicat' follow. 'praesaepia', Greenough's spelling of 'praesepia', 'stalls'. 'vinclis' = 'vinculis', syncopated like 'maniplos'. 'potitus', 'having got possession of', 'potior' with the ablative ('campo… aperto'). Homeric model: Paris running down from Troy's citadel in shining armour, compared to a stall-fed horse breaking loose for the river and the mares (Iliad VI.506–511, repeated of Hector at XV.263–268; from memory). Elision 'ub(i) abruptis'.

sentences.t:
aut ille in pastus armentaque tendit equarum
aut adsuetus aquae perfundi flumine noto
emicat adrectisque fremit cervicibus alte
luxurians, luduntque iubae per colla, per armos.
sentences.l:
either he to the pastures and the herds makes of mares,
or, used to water, to be bathed in the familiar river,
leaps out, and with neck raised snorts on high,
running riot, and play his manes over neck, over shoulders.
sentences.i: makes either for the pastures and the herds of mares, or, used to bathing in the waters of a river he knows, darts out and neighs with his neck held high, revelling, while his mane tosses over his neck and shoulders.
sentences.n: 'ille', a redundant pronoun picking up the subject, a Homeric touch. 'armenta… equarum', 'herds of mares'. 'adsuetus aquae perfundi', 'used to being bathed in water', 'aquae' probably dative with 'adsuetus', the passive infinitive in middle sense. 'emicat', 'flashes out'. 'adrectis… cervicibus', Greenough's 'arrectis', 'with neck raised'. 'luxurians', 'running riot'. 'per colla, per armos', the repeated preposition swinging like the mane. The horse is Turnus's pride and freedom; that Homer gave this simile to Paris is a sign not in his favour. Elision 'ill(e) in'.

sentences.t:
Obvia cui Volscorum acie comitante Camilla
occurrit portisque ab equo regina sub ipsis
desiluit, quam tota cohors imitata relictis
ad terram defluxit equis; tum talia fatur:
sentences.l:
Meeting him, with the Volscians' column accompanying, Camilla
runs up, and at the gates from her horse the queen, right under them,
leapt down, whom the whole troop, imitating, having left
to the ground slid down their horses; then such things she speaks:
sentences.i: To meet him came Camilla with her Volscian column at her side, and right under the gates the queen leapt down from her horse; her whole troop followed her lead, left their horses and slid to the ground; then she spoke these words:
sentences.n: 'Obvia cui', connecting relative, 'meeting him', 'obvia' predicative with 'occurrit'. Camilla, the Volscian warrior maiden, closed the catalogue of Italian forces at the end of Book VII; she is 'regina', queen of her people. 'portis… sub ipsis', 'right under the gates'. 'quam… imitata', 'imitating whom', the connecting relative again. 'relictis… equis', ablative absolute. 'defluxit', 'flowed down', a smooth dismount; to dismount was a mark of respect to a commander. 'talia fatur', the stock formula before a speech. Elisions 'Volscor(um) acie', 'portisqu(e) ab'.

sentences.t:
“Turne, sui merito siqua est fiducia forti,
audeo et Aeneadum promitto occurrere turmae
solaque Tyrrhenos equites ire obvia contra.
sentences.l:
“Turnus, if to the brave rightly there is any confidence in self,
I dare, and the sons of Aeneas I promise to meet, their squadron,
and alone the Tyrrhenian horsemen to go facing, against them.
sentences.i: “Turnus, if the brave may rightly have some confidence in themselves, I dare it, and I promise to meet the squadron of Aeneas's men, and to ride out alone against the Etruscan horsemen.
sentences.n: 'sui… fiducia', 'confidence in oneself', objective genitive; 'forti', dative of possession, 'to a brave person', a general statement that Camilla applies to herself. 'merito', 'deservedly'. 'siqua', printed as one word ('si qua'). 'Aeneadum', old genitive plural in '-um', 'of the sons of Aeneas', the Trojans. 'turmae', a cavalry squadron, dative with 'occurrere'. 'sola… obvia', feminine: Camilla speaks as a woman and as a captain. 'ire obvia contra', 'go to meet them, against them', a full, emphatic phrase. Elisions 'siqu(a) est', 'aude(o) et', 'promitt(o) occurrere', 'ir(e) obvia'.

sentences.t:
Me sine prima manu temptare pericula belli
tu pedes ad muros subsiste et moenia serva.”
sentences.l:
Me allow with my hand to try the first dangers of war;
you on foot by the walls stand fast and the defences guard.”
sentences.i: Let me put my hand to the first hazards of war, while you stay on foot by the walls and keep the defences safe.”
sentences.n: 'Me sine… temptare', 'allow me to try': 'sine' is the imperative of 'sino', 'allow', not the preposition. 'prima' is neuter plural with 'pericula', 'the first dangers of war': a feminine 'first' would have to be 'primam', agreeing with 'Me'. 'pedes', 'on foot', nominative singular of 'pedes, peditis', 'foot-soldier', not the plural of 'pes': her cavalry will meet theirs while Turnus fights as infantry at the walls. 'subsiste', 'stand fast, stay behind'. Elision 'subsist(e) et'.

sentences.t: Turnus ad haec, oculos horrenda in virgine fixus:
sentences.l: Turnus to this, his eyes on the awe-inspiring maiden fixed:
sentences.i: Turnus answered, his eyes fastened on the formidable maiden:
sentences.n: Ellipsis of the verb of speaking: 'Turnus ad haec', supply 'respondit', as often. 'oculos… fixus', 'fixed as to his eyes', the accusative with a passive participle in middle sense, like 'oculos deiecta' at 480. 'horrenda', gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be shuddered at', 'awe-inspiring': Camilla is fearsome, not merely beautiful. Elision 'horrend(a) in'.

sentences.t:
“O decus Italiae virgo, quas dicere grates
quasve referre parem?
sentences.l:
“O glory of Italy, maiden, what thanks to speak
or what to return can I provide?
sentences.i: “Maiden, glory of Italy, what thanks can I find to speak, or what to repay?
sentences.n: 'decus Italiae', 'the glory of Italy', in apposition to 'virgo'. 'grates dicere… referre', 'to say thanks… to return them': the Roman distinction between thanking in words and repaying in kind ('gratias agere', 'gratiam referre'); 'grates' is the solemn word, used of thanks to gods. 'parem', deliberative subjunctive, 'what am I to provide?'. 'quasve', '-ve', 'or'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Sed nunc, est omnia quando
iste animus supra, mecum partire laborem.
sentences.l:
But now, since above all things is
that spirit of yours, with me share the toil.
sentences.i: But now, since that spirit of yours rises above everything, share the labour with me.
sentences.n: 'est omnia quando iste animus supra': in prose order 'quando iste animus est supra omnia', 'since that courage of yours is above all things'; both 'quando' and 'supra' come after their words (anastrophe). 'iste', 'that of yours', the demonstrative of the second person. 'partire', imperative of the deponent 'partior', 'divide, share'. Turnus accepts her offer, but on his own terms. Elision 'ist(e) animus'.

sentences.t:
Aeneas, ut fama fidem missique reportant
exploratores, equitum levia improbus arma
praemisit, quaterent campos; ipse ardua montis
per deserta iugo superans adventat ad urbem.
sentences.l:
Aeneas, as rumour and the sent bring back assurance,
the scouts, of horsemen the light, the shameless one, arms
has sent ahead, to shake the plains; himself, the steep of the mountain
through the lonely places, by the ridge crossing over, approaches toward the city.
sentences.i: Aeneas, as rumour and the scouts we sent out confirm, has cunningly sent his light cavalry ahead to scour the plains, while he himself, crossing the high ground by a lonely ridge, is coming on towards the city.
sentences.n: 'ut fama fidem missique reportant exploratores', 'as rumour and the scouts sent out bring back confirmation', 'fidem reportant' with two subjects. 'improbus', 'shameless, unscrupulous', Turnus's word for an enemy's cunning. 'equitum levia… arma', 'the light arms of horsemen', for the light cavalry itself. 'quaterent campos', purpose without 'ut', 'to shake (scour) the plains'. 'ardua montis per deserta', 'through the steep, deserted places of the mountain', neuter plural adjectives used as nouns. 'iugo superans', 'passing over by the ridge'. Elisions 'levi(a) improbus', 'ips(e) ardua'.

sentences.t:
Furta paro belli convexo in tramite silvae,
ut bivias armato obsidam milite fauces.
sentences.l:
A stealth of war I prepare in the hollow track of the wood,
so that the two-way, with armed soldiery, I may beset, pass.
sentences.i: I am preparing a stratagem of war on the winding track through the forest, to hold both ends of the pass with armed men.
sentences.n: 'Furta… belli', 'thefts of war', a stratagem, an ambush; 'furtum' is anything done by stealth. 'convexo in tramite', 'on the hollow, curving path'. 'ut… obsidam', purpose clause. 'bivias… fauces', 'two-way jaws', a defile with an entrance at either end; 'fauces', 'throat', is the regular word for a narrow pass. 'armato… milite', collective singular, 'with armed soldiery'. Elisions 'convex(o) in', 'armat(o) obsidam'.

sentences.i: You must take on the Etruscan cavalry in close battle; with you will be fierce Messapus, the Latin squadrons and the troop from Tibur: you too must shoulder a general's command.”
sentences.n: 'conlatis… signis', 'with standards brought together', in pitched battle; 'conlatis' is Greenough's unassimilated 'collatis'. 'excipe', 'receive, take the shock of'. 'Tyrrhenum equitem', collective singular again. 'Tiburti… manus', 'the band of Tiburtus', the brother of Coras and Catillus after whom Tibur is named (VII.671): the men of Tibur. 'ducis… curam', 'the charge of a commander'; 'et tu', 'you too', since Turnus commands elsewhere. Turnus gives Camilla the cavalry command while he takes the ambush for himself. Elisions 'Tyrrhen(um) equitem', 'tec(um) acer'.

sentences.t:
Sic ait, et paribus Messapum in proelia dictis
hortatur sociosque duces et pergit in hostem.
sentences.l:
Thus he speaks, and with like words Messapus to battle
urges, and the allied leaders, and proceeds against the enemy.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and with like words urged Messapus and the allied captains to battle, and set out against the enemy.
sentences.n: 'Sic ait', the closing formula. 'paribus… dictis', 'with like words', framing 'Messapum in proelia'. 'socios… duces', the allied captains, Coras and Catillus among them. 'hortatur', deponent, 'urges on'. 'pergit in hostem', 'goes on against the enemy', though he is going to lie in wait rather than attack. Elision 'Messap(um) in'.

sentences.t:
Est curvo anfractu valles, adcommoda fraudi
armorumque dolis, quam densis frondibus atrum
urget utrimque latus, tenuis quo semita ducit
angustaeque ferunt fauces aditusque maligni.
sentences.l:
There is, with a curving bend, a valley, suited to stratagem
and to the tricks of arms, which, with dense leaves dark,
presses on both sides a flank, where a thin path leads
and narrow jaws bring you, and approaches grudging.
sentences.i: There is a valley with a curving bend, made for stratagems and the wiles of war, hemmed in on either side by a slope dark with thick foliage; a faint path leads into it, through a narrow gorge and a forbidding entrance.
sentences.n: 'Est… valles', 'there is a valley', the formula that opens a description of a place (compare 'Est in secessu longo locus', I.159). 'valles', an old nominative of 'vallis'. 'adcommoda', Greenough's spelling of 'accommoda', 'suited', with the datives 'fraudi… dolis'. 'quam… urget… latus', 'which a dark flank presses', 'utrimque', 'on both sides'. 'quo', 'to which', relative adverb. 'ferunt', 'lead', with no object expressed. 'maligni', 'grudging, niggardly', of an entrance that gives little room. Elision 'curv(o) anfractu'.

sentences.t:
Hanc super in speculis summoque in vertice montis
planities ignota iacet tutique receptus,
seu dextra laevaque velis occurrere pugnae,
sive instare iugis et grandia volvere saxa.
sentences.l:
Above it, among look-outs and on the highest top of the mountain,
a plain unknown lies, and safe retreats,
whether on right and left you wish to meet the fight
or to press on from the ridges and huge to roll rocks.
sentences.i: Above it, among the look-out points on the mountain's very summit, lies a hidden tableland, a safe place of retreat, whether you choose to meet the battle from right or left, or to bear down from the ridges and roll huge boulders on the enemy.
sentences.n: 'Hanc super', anastrophe, 'above this (valley)'. 'in speculis', 'on the look-outs', high points for watching. 'planities ignota', 'level ground unknown', to the enemy. 'tuti… receptus', 'safe retreats', poetic plural, nominative. 'seu… velis… sive', 'whether you wish… or', the generalising 'you', 'one'. 'occurrere pugnae', 'to meet the fight', dative. 'instare iugis', 'to press on from the ridges' or 'to take one's stand on the ridges'; either way the attack comes from above. Elisions 'summoqu(e) in', 'siv(e) instare'.

sentences.t:
Huc iuvenis nota fertur regione viarum
arripuitque locum et silvis insedit iniquis.
sentences.l:
Hither the young man by a known tract of roads is carried
and seized the place and in the woods sat down, the treacherous ones.
sentences.i: Here the young warrior hurried by a route he knew well, seized the position and settled in ambush among the treacherous woods.
sentences.n: 'Huc', 'to this place'. 'iuvenis', Turnus, still a young man. 'nota… regione viarum', 'by a known tract of roads', ablative of the way by which. 'fertur', 'is carried, hurries', passive in middle sense. 'arripuit… insedit', perfects after the present: done at once. 'silvis… iniquis', 'woods unfair', unfavourable to an enemy, a place of ambush. 'insedit', 'sat down in, occupied'. The next part turns from Turnus to Diana and the story of Camilla. Elision 'loc(um) et'.
